claim: The mammalian circadian clock exerts control of daily gene expression through cycles of DNA binding.
source: The mammalian circadian clock exerts control of daily gene expression through cycles of DNA binding.
evidence: This is a statement from the abstract that represents established understanding of circadian clock function.

claim: BMAL1 protein can regulate thousands of target sites over daily time scales.
source: Here, we develop a quantitative model of how a finite pool of BMAL1 protein can regulate thousands of target sites over daily time scales.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract describing the scope of BMAL1 regulation.

claim: Nuclear BMAL1 concentration determines corresponding CLOCK through heterodimerisation.
source: We find nuclear BMAL1 concentration determines corresponding CLOCK through heterodimerisation and define a DNA residence time of this complex.
evidence: This is a key finding from the study stated in the abstract.

claim: The DNA residence time of the CLOCK:BMAL1 complex has been defined.
source: We find nuclear BMAL1 concentration determines corresponding CLOCK through heterodimerisation and define a DNA residence time of this complex.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract.

claim: Repression of CLOCK:BMAL1 is achieved through rhythmic changes to BMAL1:CRY1 association.
source: Repression of CLOCK:BMAL1 is achieved through rhythmic changes to BMAL1:CRY1 association and high-affinity interactions between PER2:CRY1 which mediates CLOCK:BMAL1 displacement from DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study stated in the abstract.

claim: High-affinity interactions between PER2:CRY1 mediate CLOCK:BMAL1 displacement from DNA.
source: Repression of CLOCK:BMAL1 is achieved through rhythmic changes to BMAL1:CRY1 association and high-affinity interactions between PER2:CRY1 which mediates CLOCK:BMAL1 displacement from DNA.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study stated in the abstract.

claim: PER:CRY complexes have a dual role in which increasing concentrations of PER2:CRY1 promotes removal of BMAL1:CLOCK from genes and enhances ability to move to new target sites.
source: Finally, stochastic modelling reveals a dual role for PER:CRY complexes in which increasing concentrations of PER2:CRY1 promotes removal of BMAL1:CLOCK from genes consequently enhancing ability to move to new target sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from stochastic modeling stated in the abstract.

claim: Cell-autonomous circadian clocks operate in virtually all cells across tissues in mammals.
source: In mammals, cell-autonomous circadian clocks operate in virtually all cells across tissues and enables coordination of numerous biological processes, including metabolism, immunity, and cell cycle progression (Bhadra et al., 2017; Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Circadian clocks enable coordination of metabolism, immunity, and cell cycle progression.
source: In mammals, cell-autonomous circadian clocks operate in virtually all cells across tissues and enables coordination of numerous biological processes, including metabolism, immunity, and cell cycle progression (Bhadra et al., 2017; Gibbs et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: Autonomous cellular clocks are characterised by transcription-translation feedback loops (TTFLs).
source: Autonomous cellular clocks are characterised by transcription-translation feedback loops (TTFLs), leading to cycles in protein and mRNA tuned to the 24 hr rhythms of the day-night cycle.
evidence: This is established knowledge about circadian clock mechanisms.

claim: CLOCK:BMAL1 heterodimer searches the genome to bind consensus sequence E-box sites (CANNTG).
source: Central to the mammalian circadian clock is the heterodimeric transcription factor comprised of CLOCK (circadian locomotor output cycles protein kaput) and BMAL1 (brain and muscle ARNT-like 1) that searches the genome to bind consensus sequence E-box sites (CANNTG), inducing expression of several hundred clock-controlled output genes every day.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CLOCK:BMAL1 function.

claim: CLOCK:BMAL1 induces expression of several hundred clock-controlled output genes every day.
source: Central to the mammalian circadian clock is the heterodimeric transcription factor comprised of CLOCK (circadian locomotor output cycles protein kaput) and BMAL1 (brain and muscle ARNT-like 1) that searches the genome to bind consensus sequence E-box sites (CANNTG), inducing expression of several hundred clock-controlled output genes every day.
evidence: This is established knowledge about CLOCK:BMAL1 function.

claim: CLOCK:BMAL1 targets include key circadian negative feedback regulators Period (Per1, Per2, Per3) and Cryptochrome (Cry1 and Cry2).
source: Targets include key circadian negative feedback regulators, Period (Per1, Per2, Per3), Cryptochrome (Cry1 and Cry2) and a secondary loop regulated by Nr1d1 and Nr1d2 (Buhr and Takahashi, 2013; Gekakis et al., 1998; Huang et al., 2012; Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by multiple citations to previous literature.

claim: PER and CRY proteins dimerise to form a repressive complex with CK1 to promote removal of CLOCK:BMAL1 from DNA.
source: In a current model, it is proposed that PER and CRY proteins dimerise to form a repressive complex with CK1 (casein kinase 1) to promote the removal of CLOCK:BMAL1 from DNA and thereby repress transactivation of target genes, while CRY1 independently binds the PAS domain core of CLOCK:BMAL1 and the BMAL1 transactivation domain leaving DNA binding intact whilst repressing recruitment of additional transcriptional coactivators (Chiou et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a current model supported by citations.

claim: CRY1 independently binds the PAS domain core of CLOCK:BMAL1 and the BMAL1 transactivation domain leaving DNA binding intact whilst repressing recruitment of additional transcriptional coactivators.
source: In a current model, it is proposed that PER and CRY proteins dimerise to form a repressive complex with CK1 (casein kinase 1) to promote the removal of CLOCK:BMAL1 from DNA and thereby repress transactivation of target genes, while CRY1 independently binds the PAS domain core of CLOCK:BMAL1 and the BMAL1 transactivation domain leaving DNA binding intact whilst repressing recruitment of additional transcriptional coactivators (Chiou et al., 2016; Xu et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a current model supported by citations.

claim: REV-ERBα operates as a transcriptional repressor of Bmal1, resulting in a cycle of BMAL1 protein abundance.
source: An additional feedback loop is conferred by the protein REV-ERBα, which operates as a transcriptional repressor of Bmal1, resulting in a cycle of BMAL1 protein abundance (Liu et al., 2008).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: PER2 was found to cycle with a maximum amplitude of 12,000 copies per cell in fibroblasts.
source: PER2 was found to cycle with a maximum amplitude of 12,000 copies per cell in fibroblasts and without circadian gating of nuclear localisation, contrary to observations in the Drosophila clock (Shafer et al., 2002; Smyllie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work by the authors, supported by citation.

claim: PER2 does not exhibit circadian gating of nuclear localisation in mammalian cells, contrary to observations in the Drosophila clock.
source: PER2 was found to cycle with a maximum amplitude of 12,000 copies per cell in fibroblasts and without circadian gating of nuclear localisation, contrary to observations in the Drosophila clock (Shafer et al., 2002; Smyllie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a finding from previous work, supported by citations.

claim: Only a relatively small amount of CRY1 is needed to localise PER2 to the nucleus.
source: Only a relatively small amount of CRY1 is needed to localise PER2 to the nucleus, as shown in live SCN studies, with PER2 localisation remaining predominantly nuclear throughout the day (Smyllie et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: PER2 localisation remains predominantly nuclear throughout the day.
source: Only a relatively small amount of CRY1 is needed to localise PER2 to the nucleus, as shown in live SCN studies, with PER2 localisation remaining predominantly nuclear throughout the day (Smyllie et al., 2022).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous work.

claim: CRY1 protein remains nuclear at all circadian phases in U20S cancer cell line.
source: A recent study using a cancer cell line model has also shown that CRY1 protein remains nuclear at all circadian phases and at markedly higher abundance than its partner protein PER2 (Gabriel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: CRY1 is at markedly higher abundance than PER2 in U20S cancer cell line.
source: A recent study using a cancer cell line model has also shown that CRY1 protein remains nuclear at all circadian phases and at markedly higher abundance than its partner protein PER2 (Gabriel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to previous literature.

claim: High-affinity interactions between circadian protein complexes serve to offset the low abundances of circadian proteins.
source: Using a combination of mathematical modelling and experimental validation, our data reveal that high-affinity interactions between circadian protein complexes serve to offset the low abundances of circadian proteins.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study combining modeling and experiments.

claim: The abundance of key components of the molecular clockwork is positioned optimally to regulate E-box binding.
source: In this way, the abundance of key components of the molecular clockwork is positioned optimally to regulate E-box binding.
evidence: This is an inference from the study's findings.

claim: PER2 protein serves a dual role, acting as both a component of the negative feedback arm and to redistribute CLOCK:BMAL1 to new target sites.
source: This is partly facilitated through PER2:CRY1 mediated displacement of CLOCK:BMAL1, such that PER2 protein serves a dual role, acting as both a component of the negative feedback arm but also to redistribute CLOCK:BMAL1 to new target sites.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the study.

claim: The stochiometric balance of PER:CRY with CLOCK:BMAL1 is critical for the elucidation of the full cellular circadian repertoire.
source: Thus, the stochiometric balance of PER:CRY with CLOCK:BMAL1 is critical for the elucidation of the full cellular circadian repertoire.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Expression of the BMAL1::EGFP transgene was in >10 fold excess over the native unfused protein.
source: Expression of the transgene was in >10 fold excess over the native unfused protein, as determined by single molecule Fluorescence In Situ Hybridisation (Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is a measurement from the study using smFISH, with reference to a figure.

claim: BMAL1 expression is strongly localised to the nucleus.
source: Confocal microscopy of tagRFP::CLOCK or BMAL1::EGFP showed BMAL1 expression to be strongly localised to the nucleus, whereas CLOCK was predominantly cytoplasmic when expressed alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy with reference to a figure.

claim: CLOCK is predominantly cytoplasmic when expressed alone.
source: Confocal microscopy of tagRFP::CLOCK or BMAL1::EGFP showed BMAL1 expression to be strongly localised to the nucleus, whereas CLOCK was predominantly cytoplasmic when expressed alone (Figure 1C).
evidence: This is an observation from confocal microscopy with reference to a figure.

claim: Co-expression of BMAL1 and CLOCK causes localisation of tagRFP::CLOCK to move to the nucleus.
source: Co-expression of both proteins in the same cells caused localisation of tagRFP::CLOCK to move to the nucleus, in agreement with earlier studies which showed cytoplasmic CLOCK localisation in BMAL1-deficient cells, and that circadian regulation of nuclear localisation of CLOCK correlated with BMAL1 availability (Kondratov et al., 2003; Stratmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The BMAL1 L95E DNA-binding mutant re-localised tagRFP::CLOCK protein to the nucleus from the cytoplasm in a manner equivalent to WT BMAL1.
source: The mutant BMAL1 also re-localised tagRFP::CLOCK protein to the nucleus from the cytoplasm in an manner equivalent to WT BMAL1 (Figure 1C; Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an observation from the study with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: BMAL1 recovery half-life is insensitive to the diameter of the bleached region, indicating that binding contributes to the recovery profile.
source: BMAL1 recovery half-life was found to be insensitive to the diameter of the bleached region, indicating that binding contributes to the recovery profile rather than this being a solely diffusion-led process (Figure 1—figure supplement 2; Sprague and McNally, 2005).
evidence: This is a finding from FRAP experiments with reference to a figure and citation.

claim: Residence time of BMAL1::EGFP was increased in the presence of tagRFP::CLOCK (p < 0.0001).
source: Residence time of BMAL1::EGFP was increased in the presence of tagRFP::CLOCK (p < 0.0001), consistent with a requirement for CLOCK to bind DNA (Figure 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from FRAP experiments with statistical significance and reference to a figure.

claim: The mean residence time for the fluorescent CLOCK:BMAL1 complex was 4.13 s (95% CI, 0.57).
source: The mean residence time for the fluorescent CLOCK:BMAL1 complex was 4.13 s (95% CI, 0.57), a value consistent with DNA residence times for similar transcription factors (Hettich and Gebhardt, 2018; Stratmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a measurement from the study, supported by citations to previous literature.

claim: The BMAL1 L95E mutant exhibited a significantly reduced residence time of 2.83 s (95% CI, 0.54; p = 0.0002).
source: Using the L95E DNA-binding mutant protein, we saw significantly reduced residence time of 2.83 s (95% CI, 0.54; p = 0.0002).
evidence: This is a measurement from the study with statistical significance.

claim: The BMAL1 L95E mutant showed a twofold reduction in PER2::LUC expression.
source: Notably, the initial publication of the BMAL1 L95E mutant showed a twofold reduction in PER2::LUC expression and so suggests a strong relationship between DNA binding and transcriptional output (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: The L95E mutant diffused more rapidly than WT BMAL1, consistent with fewer interactions with DNA in the nucleus.
source: The L95E mutant diffused more rapidly than WT BMAL1, consistent with fewer interactions with DNA in the nucleus (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is an observation from FCS experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: When co-expressed, WT BMAL1 and CLOCK exhibited a 2:1 concentration ratio in the nucleus.
source: When co-expressed, WT BMAL1 and CLOCK exhibited a 2:1 concentration ratio in the nucleus (Figure 2D, Figure 2—figure supplement 2E), presumably arising from a combination of differences in protein turnover, shuttling and direct interaction.
evidence: This is a measurement from FCS experiments with reference to figures.

claim: The V435R mutation of BMAL1 leads to reduced dimerisation with CLOCK.
source: Previous work found that the V435R mutation of BMAL1 in the PAS-B domain, leads to reduced dimerisation with CLOCK (Huang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a finding from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: The BMAL1 L95E DNA binding mutant showed no difference in interaction affinity compared to WT BMAL1 protein.
source: In contrast, the BMAL1 L95E DNA binding mutant showed no difference in interaction affinity compared to WT BMAL1 protein.
evidence: This is a finding from FCCS experiments.

claim: BMAL1 is a critical determinant of the localisation, mobility and concentration of CLOCK in the nucleus.
source: These data demonstrate that BMAL1 is a critical determinant of the localisation, mobility and concentration of CLOCK in the nucleus.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental findings.

claim: Total copies of endogenous BMAL1 per nucleus vary from 1000 to 10,000 between individual cells.
source: We also measured protein number of the endogenous BMAL1, observing that total copies per nucleus vary from 1000 to 10,000 between individual cells, likely due to desynchrony and differing nuclear volumes.
evidence: This is a measurement from the study using endogenously labeled mice.

claim: CRY1::mRuby3 fluorescence in SCN slices exhibited regular cycles with a period of 23.9 hr (SD, 0.6).
source: First, to test any potential impact on circadian pace-making, we measured CRY1::mRuby3 fluorescence in whole-field organotypic SCN slices (Figure 3—figure supplement 3B) which exhibited regular cycles in red fluorescence with a period of 23.9 hr (SD, 0.6) (Figure 3—figure supplement 3C; Smyllie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a measurement from SCN slice imaging with reference to figures.

claim: Lung fibroblasts from BMAL1xCRY1 mice exhibited bioluminescence cycles of 23.3 hr (SD, 0.6) sustained for >4 days.
source: Using isolated lung fibroblasts from BMAL1xCRY1 mice we assessed bioluminescence in response to dexamethasone (DEX) synchronisation, and observed 23.3 hr cycles (SD, 0.6) which were sustained for >4 days (Figure 3—figure supplement Figure 3—figure supplement 3D, E).
evidence: This is a measurement from bioluminescence recordings with reference to figures.

claim: Peak protein concentrations of BMAL1 and CRY1 had an approximate phase-separation of 8 hr.
source: Peak protein concentrations of BMAL1 and CRY1 had an approximate and appropriate phase-separation of 8 hr (Fustin et al., 2009).
evidence: This is an observation from the study, supported by citation.

claim: The mean interaction strength between BMAL1 and CRY1 is >2 fold stronger than that between BMAL1 and CLOCK.
source: Intriguingly, the mean interaction strength between BMAL1 and CRY1 is >2 fold stronger than that between BMAL1 and CLOCK (Figure 2G).
evidence: This is a comparison of measurements from FCCS experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: PER2 was found to have the slowest diffusion coefficient recorded within all FCS measurements.
source: PER2 was found to have the slowest diffusion coefficient recorded within all our F(C)CS measurements, when in the non-aggregate space.
evidence: This is an observation from FCS experiments.

claim: PER2 mobility was not altered following co-expression with CRY1.
source: PER2 mobility was not altered following co-expression with CRY1, whereas CRY1 exhibited reduced mobility in the presence of ectopic EGFP::PER2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from FCS experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: CRY1 exhibited reduced mobility in the presence of ectopic EGFP::PER2.
source: PER2 mobility was not altered following co-expression with CRY1, whereas CRY1 exhibited reduced mobility in the presence of ectopic EGFP::PER2 (Figure 4B).
evidence: This is an observation from FCS experiments with reference to a figure.

claim: Predicted DNA binding of CLOCK:BMAL1 has an average baseline of 194 sites bound at any one time, rising to 526 sites at the peak.
source: Furthermore, predicted DNA binding of CLOCK:BMAL1 has an average baseline of 194 sites bound at any one time, rising to 526 sites at the peak, in agreement with the expected ≈2-fold peak enrichment from ChIP reports (Beytebiere et al., 2019; Koike et al., 2012; Figure 5E).
evidence: This is an inference from the ODE model, supported by citations and reference to a figure.

claim: DNA-bound CLOCK:BMAL1:CRY1 complex was persistent, with low abundance cycling from 32 to 69 target sites (accounting for 11% of total BMAL1 bound sites).
source: Finally, DNA-bound CLOCK:BMAL1:CRY1 complex was persistent, with low abundance cycling from 32 to 69 target sites (accounting for 11% of total BMAL1 bound sites).
evidence: This is an inference from the ODE model.

claim: Target site occupancy decreased marginally from 16.2% to 13.6% when varying binding sites from 1000 to 10,000.
source: We found target site occupancy decreased marginally from 16.2% to 13.6%, showing that any variance between different numbers of available target sites has minimal impact.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis of the model.

claim: The CLOCK:BMAL1 unbinding rate accounted for a 21.5% change when residence times across the observed physiological range are considered.
source: The CLOCK:BMAL1 unbinding rate accounted for a 21.5% change when residence times across the observed physiological range are considered (Figure 6B); outside of this range occupancy begins to saturate so that a further 30 s increase in residence time only accounts for an additional 12.5% binding.
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analysis of the model with reference to a figure.

claim: The unbinding rate is optimally positioned to regulate target site occupancy in a manner consistent with the displacement mechanism governed by PER:CRY.
source: Therefore, the unbinding rate, as measured experimentally, is optimally positioned to regulate target site occupancy in a manner consistent with the displacement mechanism governed by PER:CRY.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from sensitivity analysis.

claim: At T40, 95% of the 3,436 target sites would be bound at least once within a minute.
source: At T40, when there is the maximum amount of CLOCK:BMAL1, 95% of the 3,436 target sites would be bound at least once within a minute, changing to ca. 2 minutes at T28 (Figure 7B), contributing towards a small degree of heterogeneity.
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling with reference to a figure.

claim: From the perspective of a single promoter at T40 there are ≈3.2 visits per minute by CLOCK:BMAL1, which is reduced down to ≈1.4 visits per minute at T28.
source: From the perspective of a single promoter at T40 there are ≈3.2 visits per minute by CLOCK:BMAL1, which is reduced down to ≈1.4 visits per minute at T28 (Figure 7C), with further reductions in individual cells with lower concentrations of CLOCK:BMAL1 protein (Figure 7—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling with reference to figures.

claim: CLOCK:BMAL1:CRY1 complex makes up ≈15% of total visits to target sites.
source: We then separated the total visits per minute into those occurring as CLOCK:BMAL1 compared to those occurring as the CLOCK:BMAL1:CRY1 complex, finding the latter to remain relatively persistent across time points and making up ≈15% of total visits, mirroring results for our ODE model.
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling.

claim: Changing BMAL1 protein abundance accounts for the most variation in number of target site visitations, changing from 1.3 visits at the nadir to 2.7 visits at peak BMAL1 protein.
source: We find that changing BMAL1 protein abundance accounts for the most variation in number of target site visitations, changing from 1.3 visits at the nadir to 2.7 visits at peak BMAL1 protein (Figure 7E).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling with reference to a figure.

claim: CLOCK:BMAL1 mobility is supported by the action of PER2:CRY1 across all time points, accounting for a maximum 15% of visits at the trough of PER2 protein levels (T40).
source: CLOCK:BMAL1 mobility is supported by the action of PER2:CRY1 across all time points, accounting for a maximum 15% of visits at the trough of PER2 protein levels (T40).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling.

claim: In the complete absence of PER2, BMAL1 mobility is hampered so that it visits less than three sites per minute.
source: In the complete absence of PER2, BMAL1 mobility is hampered so that it visits less than three sites per minute.
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling.

claim: When PER2 spans the physiological range and beyond, a strong relationship in the visits per minute is forecast, rising by a third and in the opposite relationship to site occupancy.
source: When PER2 spans the physiological range and beyond, a strong relationship in the visits per minute is forecast, rising by a third and in the opposite relationship to site occupancy.
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling.

claim: PER2 acts both as part of a transcriptional repressor complex and as a facilitator of CLOCK:BMAL1 mobility to bind new target sites.
source: In this sense, PER2 acts both as part of a transcriptional repressor complex and as a facilitator of CLOCK:BMAL1 mobility to bind new target sites (Cao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a conclusion from the study, supported by citation.

claim: Low molecular abundances of core circadian components lead to rapid internal and cell-to-cell desynchrony.
source: Mathematical modelling demonstrates that low molecular abundances, as observed for core circadian components, lead to rapid internal and cell-to-cell desynchrony, which may be compensated for by strict control of stoichiometries and interactions (Gonze and Goldbeter, 2006).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous modeling work.

claim: Approximately 16,000 BMAL1 proteins per nucleus were found in lung fibroblasts.
source: We found approximately 16,000 BMAL1 and 8000 CRY1 proteins per nucleus, consistent with our earlier reports for PER2 which found 12,000 proteins per nucleus in skin fibroblasts (Smyllie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a measurement from the study.

claim: Approximately 8000 CRY1 proteins per nucleus were found in lung fibroblasts.
source: We found approximately 16,000 BMAL1 and 8000 CRY1 proteins per nucleus, consistent with our earlier reports for PER2 which found 12,000 proteins per nucleus in skin fibroblasts (Smyllie et al., 2016).
evidence: This is a measurement from the study.

claim: Gabriel et al. found approximately an eight-fold difference between CRY1 and PER2 using the U20S osteocarcinoma cancer cell line.
source: Interestingly, a recent study by Gabriel et al. found approximately an eight-fold difference between CRY1 and PER2 using the U20S, osteocarinoma cancer cell line, highlighting how different cell types and cell lines may diverge and influence the circadian network (Gabriel et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Fibroblasts exhibited a > 2 fold increase in BMAL1 concentration when compared with chondrocytes.
source: Similarly, we observed significant disparities of endogenous BMAL1 across a range of cell types, with fibroblasts exhibiting a > 2 fold increase in BMAL1 concentration when compared with chondrocytes (Figure 3—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a measurement from the study with reference to a figure.

claim: Only 10% of BMAL1 was bound in complex with CLOCK.
source: Strikingly, only 10% of BMAL1 was bound in complex with CLOCK.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: Low availability of heterodimeric transcription factor for DNA interactions is compatible with allowing other interactions to occur, including those reported with HIF and AhR.
source: Low availability of heterodimeric transcription factor for DNA interactions, when compared with free protein, severely limits the potential to bind DNA, yet this is consistent with allowing other interactions to occur, including those reported with Hypoxia-inducible factor (HIF) and Aryl hydrocarbon receptor (AhR) (Bagnall et al., 2014; Jaeger and Tischkau, 2016).
evidence: This is an interpretation supported by citations.

claim: The interaction between BMAL1 and CRY1 is not only rhythmic but remarkably strong, with a higher affinity than any other protein pairings measured.
source: Here, we have shown in live cells that this interaction is not only rhythmic but remarkably strong, with a higher affinity than any other protein pairings we have measured.
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: When acting without PER2, CRY1 exhibits near-persistent repression over 24 hr.
source: When acting without PER2, CRY1 exhibits near-persistent repression over 24 hr, likely owing to its regulated interaction with CLOCK and BMAL1, as evidenced by modelling the effect of removal of either cycling BMAL1, CRY1 or binding affinity between the two (Figure 3F, Figure 5—figure supplement 1F).
evidence: This is a finding from modeling with reference to figures.

claim: The mammalian circadian clock relies on oscillations in the ability of key proteins to heterodimerise one another.
source: This cycle in affinity provides evidence that the mammalian circadian clock also relies on oscillations in the ability of key proteins to heterodimerise one another.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the findings.

claim: An average short residence time of 3 s was found for CLOCK:BMAL1, similar to other DNA binding transcription factors including GR, p53, p65, and STAT1.
source: We found an average short residence time of 3 s for CLOCK:BMAL1, similar to other DNA binding transcription factors including GR, p53, p65, and STAT1 (Hettich and Gebhardt, 2018), potentially optimised to reduce gene expression noise (Azpeitia and Wagner, 2020).
evidence: This is a finding from the study, supported by citations.

claim: Robustly detected peaks found by ChIP-seq represent genes with a slow unbinding rate.
source: Presumably, robustly detected peaks found by ChiP-seq represent genes with a slow unbinding rate, such as the E-box sites found in the DBP gene, which is supported by previous live cell imaging characterising a longer 8-s residence time for BMAL1 on a DBP E-box concatemer (Stratmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is an inference supported by citation.

claim: BMAL1 protein remains as high as 10,000 molecules per nucleus even at the nadir of expression.
source: Daily changes in BMAL1 protein are moderate, remaining as high as 10,000 molecules per nucleus even at the nadir of expression, resulting in many non-transcriptionally productive interactions of CLOCK:BMAL1 with DNA throughout the circadian cycle; these interactions however may be important, contributing to pioneer factor activity and allowing others genes to activate at a different phase to BMAL1 protein levels (Klemz et al., 2021; Menet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is a finding from the study.

claim: PER2 removes CLOCK:BMAL1 in a CRY-dependent manner from E-Boxes via recruitment of CK1 and subsequent phosphorylation of CLOCK.
source: Work by Cao and Wang et al revealed PER2 removes CLOCK:BMAL1 in a CRY-dependent manner from E-Boxes via recruitment of CK1 and subsequent phosphorylation of CLOCK, effectively reducing affinity for DNA (Cao et al., 2021).
evidence: This is a finding from previous literature, supported by citation.

claim: Reducing residency time increases the rate at which a limited pool of transcription factors can move onto new sites.
source: However, reducing residency time increases the rate at which a limited pool of transcription factors can move onto new sites, hence increasing the likelihood of any one gene to be bound and reducing possible cell-to-cell variation.
evidence: This is a logical inference from the findings.

claim: Groups of genes have maximal CLOCK:BMAL1 binding events outside of the zenith of total genome CLOCK:BMAL1 binding.
source: This supports findings by Menet and colleagues, who highlight groups of genes that have maximal binding events, as determined via ChIP-seq, outside of the zenith of total genome CLOCK:BMAL1 binding (Menet et al., 2014).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: CLOCK:BMAL1 behaves as a 'kamikaze' transcription factor, most transcriptionally potent when phosphorylated and marked for degradation.
source: Furthermore, evidence of CLOCK:BMAL1 behaving as a so-called 'kamikaze' transcription factor, a factor most transcriptionally potent when phosphorylated and marked for degradation, implies that in addition to an increase in visitations per minute, transcriptional potency is also upregulated (Stratmann et al., 2012).
evidence: This is supported by citation to previous literature.

claim: PER:CRY displacement played a significant role, contributing to 15% of visitations per minutes at the height of DNA binding and CLOCK:BMAL1 concentration (T40).
source: PER:CRY displacement played a significant role, even at its nadir of expression, contributing to 15% of visitations per minutes at the height of DNA binding and CLOCK:BMAL1 concentration (T40).
evidence: This is a finding from stochastic modeling.
